scenes.title: What F = ma means

beats.text: Newton’s second law says: resultant force equals mass times acceleration.
Use force in newtons, mass in kilograms, and acceleration in metres per second squared.
F means the combined effect of all the forces on this one body. Opposing forces subtract.
If they balance, the resultant is zero, so acceleration is zero. A moving car keeps a constant velocity.
Newton’s third law pairs forces on different bodies. They do not cancel on this car’s force diagram.

scenes.title: Direction and weight

beats.text: Take right as positive. This car moves right, but braking slows it down.
Acceleration points left, so it is negative, even while the car moves right.
Mass is not weight. Weight is the downward force of gravity: W equals m g.
Now consider a particle hanging from a taut string, accelerating upwards. Take up as positive: tension acts up and weight acts down.
Apply the law upwards: tension minus m g equals m a.
At constant velocity, a is zero, so tension equals weight. With upward acceleration, tension must be greater than weight.

scenes.title: Picture the whole journey

beats.text: Consider a car waiting on a straight, horizontal road.
It starts from rest. The engine drives it forward, while resistance acts backwards.
The forward force is larger. Watch it speed up, covering more ground in equal times.
We will find its acceleration, then how far it travels during the first few seconds.

scenes.title: The whole question

beats.text: Model the car as a particle of constant mass, twelve hundred kilograms.
Its constant driving force is three thousand newtons to the right.
The total resistance is a constant six hundred newtons to the left.
It starts from rest: initial velocity, u, is zero.
We consider the first four seconds on the straight, horizontal road.
Find the acceleration, a, and the distance travelled, s.
beats.caption: Find a and s.

scenes.title: First, find the acceleration

beats.text: Choose right as positive. The forces are constant, so the acceleration will be constant too.
Start with the law: resultant force equals mass times acceleration.
Driving force minus resistance equals mass times acceleration. We subtract because the forces oppose each other.
The driving force is three thousand newtons.
Subtract six hundred newtons of resistance.
Set that equal to twelve hundred times a.
The resultant is twenty-four hundred newtons to the right.
Divide by the mass to isolate acceleration: twenty-four hundred divided by twelve hundred.
So a equals two metres per second squared, to the right.
Each second, the velocity increases by two metres per second. This is a change in velocity, not the velocity itself.

scenes.title: Then, find the distance

beats.text: Acceleration links Newton’s second law to suvat, for the same four seconds.
To find distance from u, a and t, choose s equals u t plus one half a t squared.
From rest, initial velocity is zero.
Time is four seconds.
And acceleration is two metres per second squared.
Substitute: zero times four, plus one half times two times four squared.
Four squared is sixteen; one half times two is one.
The distance travelled is sixteen metres.
Since the car moves only right, distance equals positive displacement.
Increase resistance, keeping it below the same driving force: what changes? The smaller resultant gives less acceleration and less distance.

scenes.title: Check your understanding

beats.text: A moving car now has equal forward and backward forces. Must it stop? Take a moment.
No. Zero resultant means zero acceleration, so its existing velocity stays constant.
Use the resultant force.
